metadata.title: A Machine-Learning Approach to Predicting the Achievement of Australian Students Using School Climate; Learner Characteristics; and Economic, Social, and Cultural Status

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses OECD PISA 2022 microdata for Australia, with 15-year-old students nested within schools. The manuscript reports a stratified random split into 70% training and 30% testing sets, but it does not report whether OECD/PISA sampling weights (and any replicate weights) were applied in model estimation or evaluation. Because the analysis is based on standard ML regressors (SVM, KNN, Decision Tree, Elastic Net, XGBoost) implemented in R/Python, the paper does not describe any weight-aware estimation; this suggests weights may have been omitted or not discussed. For replication with PISA, analysts should use the appropriate PISA student sampling weights (and replicate weights if variance estimation is required) and ensure that any preprocessing (e.g., scaling/tuning) is performed within resampling folds to respect the complex survey design.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper predicts mathematics achievement from PISA 2022 and reports regression performance metrics, but it does not describe how missing values were handled (e.g., complete-case deletion vs. imputation) or how PISA plausible values were incorporated into the regression workflow. Given that PISA achievement is typically represented using plausible values, the absence of explicit PV and missing-data documentation is a reporting gap that limits interpretability and reproducibility of the ML results. This is especially important because different PV pooling strategies can change both point estimates and uncertainty.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used OECD PISA 2022 data for Australia, focusing on 15-year-old students’ mathematics achievement and questionnaire-derived constructs representing school climate, learner characteristics, and ESCS. The manuscript reports that 13,437 students in 743 schools completed the assessments, representing an estimated 90% of the total student population for this cohort. For ML modeling, the dataset was split into 70% training and 30% testing using a stratified random sampling approach to preserve proportional representation of classes; no additional inclusion/exclusion rules (e.g., missingness thresholds, outlier removal) are specified.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Best model: XGBoost — MSE: 5227.0, RMSE: 72.776, MAE: 57.67, MAPE: 0.125, R2: 0.424 (adjusted R2 highest), correlation coefficient: 0.6577. Friedman test: statistic 29.49, p-value 0.00004922; Nemenyi critical difference 1.39.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Australia (15-year-olds) mathematics achievement the study leveraged mathematics self-efficacy, socioeconomic status (ESCS), student–teacher interaction, sense of belonging, and disciplinary climate to predict mathematics achievement, finding that XGBoost achieved the lowest prediction errors (MSE 5227.0; RMSE 72.776) and the highest fit (R2 0.424; correlation 0.6577) among the five regressors. This indicates that strengthening mathematics self-efficacy and addressing socioeconomic disadvantage—alongside improving teacher-student interaction and classroom climate—may be promising targets for school improvement, while also noting that SHAP-based feature importance is predictive rather than causal and the paper does not fully document PV/missing-data handling.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses OECD PISA 2022 microdata for Australia (13,437 students in 743 schools; 15-year-olds) to predict mathematics achievement from school climate, learner characteristics, and ESCS. Five regression ML models were compared using a stratified 70/30 train-test split and hyperparameter tuning, with performance evaluated via MSE, RMSE, MAE, MAPE, R², and correlation. XGBoost was the best-performing model, achieving MSE = 5227.0, RMSE = 72.776, MAE = 57.67, MAPE = 0.125, and R² = 0.424 (correlation coefficient = 0.6577), and it significantly outperformed other models in a Friedman test (p = 0.00004922). SHAP interpretation suggests mathematics self-efficacy (MATHEFF) and ESCS are the strongest predictors, with additional feature interactions (MATHEFF×ESCS). Limitations include lack of explicit documentation of plausible-value pooling and missing-data handling, and SHAP explanations do not establish causal effects.
